guide.title: Unit 4: Data Collections: review guide
guide.intro: This is the largest unit on the exam. It covers storing many values in arrays, ArrayList objects, and 2D arrays; the standard algorithms that traverse them; reading data from text files; wrapper classes; searching, sorting, and recursion; and the ethical issues that come with collecting and using data. Two of the four free-response questions (ArrayList and 2D array) come from here.

sections.title: Data sets, ethics, text files, and wrapper classes
body: Programs that collect data put personal privacy at risk, so programmers should safeguard it. Algorithmic bias is systematic, repeated error that produces unfair outcomes for a group of users; it can come from how a data set was collected. Data sets can be incomplete or inaccurate, and a data set gathered for one question may not be appropriate for answering another.

A file stores data that persists after a program ends. To read a text file, create a File from its name and pass it to a Scanner; the File and IOException classes need an import from java.io, and the method header must say throws IOException. Scanner methods include nextInt, nextDouble, nextBoolean, next, nextLine, hasNext (used as a while-loop condition), and close. String's split(del) returns an array of the pieces of a string around a delimiter.

Integer and Double are immutable wrapper classes for int and double. Autoboxing converts a primitive to its wrapper automatically (for example, when adding an int to an ArrayList<Integer>), and unboxing converts back. Integer.parseInt(s) and Double.parseDouble(s) convert strings to numbers.
points: A data set answers only the questions it was collected to answer.
while (in.hasNext()) reads until the file has no more data.

sections.title: Arrays
body: An array holds a fixed number of values of one type; its size is set when it is created and is given by its length attribute. new int[5] creates an array whose elements have default values (0, 0.0, false, or null); an initializer list such as {4, 8, 15} gives the values directly. Valid indices run from 0 to length - 1; any other index throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

A traversal visits the elements with a loop. An indexed for loop can read and change elements. An enhanced for loop gives a copy of each element in turn, so assigning to its variable does not change the array (though methods called on an object element do change that object). Standard algorithms: minimum or maximum, sum or average, whether at least one or all elements have a property, counting, consecutive pairs, duplicates, shifting or rotating elements, and reversing.
points: for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) visits every index.
Assigning to an enhanced for loop variable never changes the array.

sections.title: ArrayList
body: An ArrayList<E> is a resizable list of object references; it needs import java.util.ArrayList. Methods: size(); add(obj), which appends; add(index, obj), which inserts and shifts later elements right; get(index); set(index, obj), which replaces an element and returns the old one; and remove(index), which removes an element, shifts later elements left, and returns the removed element. Indices run from 0 to size() - 1; others throw an IndexOutOfBoundsException.

Removing elements while traversing forward skips the element that slides into the removed position; traverse backward, or do not advance the index after a removal. Adding or removing during an enhanced for loop can throw a ConcurrentModificationException. The standard array algorithms also apply to lists, and some algorithms traverse two lists or arrays at once.
points: Arrays use length and [i]; lists use size(), get(i), and set(i, x).
To remove while traversing, loop from the last index down to 0.

sections.title: 2D arrays
body: A 2D array is an array of arrays. arr[r][c] is the element in row r and column c; arr.length is the number of rows, and arr[0].length is the number of columns (only rectangular 2D arrays are used). arr[r] is the 1D array for row r. An initializer list such as {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}} has one inner list per row.

Nested loops traverse a 2D array. Row-major order puts the row loop outside and visits each row left to right; column-major order puts the column loop outside. In a nested enhanced for loop, the outer variable is a row (a 1D array) and the inner variable is an element. The standard algorithms can be applied to the whole array or to a single row or column.

sections.title: Searching, sorting, and recursion
body: Linear search checks each element in order until the target is found or the elements run out; it works on unsorted data. Binary search requires sorted data: it checks the middle element and discards half of the remaining elements each time, so it is usually much faster. Selection sort repeatedly selects the smallest (or largest) element of the unsorted part and swaps it into its final position. Insertion sort takes the next unsorted element and inserts it into its place in the sorted part by shifting larger elements over. Merge sort divides the array into halves until each piece has one element and then merges the sorted pieces.

A recursive method calls itself. It needs a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive call that moves toward the base case; each call has its own parameters and local variables. To trace one, write out each call until the base case and then work back, combining the returned values. Recursion can traverse strings, arrays, and lists, and binary search and merge sort are often written recursively. Writing recursive code is outside the AP exam; tracing it is not.
points: Trace recursion down to the base case, then back up.

example.prompt: What does this code segment print?  ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<Integer>();  list.add(4); list.add(9); list.add(0, 7); list.remove(1);  System.out.println(list + " " + list.size());
example.solution: After the first two adds the list is [4, 9]. add(0, 7) inserts 7 at the front: [7, 4, 9]. remove(1) removes the element at index 1, which is 4: [7, 9]. The output is [7, 9] 2.

misconceptions: The last element is arr[arr.length - 1]; arr[arr.length] throws an exception.
“An enhanced for loop can change the values stored in an array of ints.”
Its variable holds a copy of each element.
It works only when the data are sorted.
The first index is the row and the second is the column.

50.5 leaves out the + 8; n is 50, and 50 + 2.5 is 52.5.

questions.prompt: Which loop removes every negative value from an ArrayList<Integer> named list without skipping any element?
choices: for (int i = 0; i <= list.size(); i++) { if (list.get(i) < 0) { list.remove(i); } }
for (int i = list.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { if (list.get(i) < 0) { list.remove(i); } }
for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) { if (list.get(i) < 0) { list.remove(i); } }
questions.explanation: Traversing from the last index down to 0 means a removal shifts only elements that have already been checked.
choiceExplanations: i <= list.size() reaches an index that does not exist and throws an exception.
Changing the size of a list inside an enhanced for loop can throw a ConcurrentModificationException.
Going forward, the element that slides into a removed position is skipped.

Divide the array in half until each piece has one element, then merge the pieces in sorted order.
Take each element in turn and insert it into its place among the elements before it.
Repeatedly find the smallest remaining element and swap it into its final position.
questions.explanation: Merge sort is a recursive divide-and-merge algorithm.
choiceExplanations: That describes binary search, which finds a value rather than sorting.
That describes insertion sort.
That describes selection sort.
